Daniel’s post presents the mix as a finished object but withholds the one thing that would let a reader *hear it as an argument*: a claim about why these two cultural artifacts belong in the same sonic frame. “Cups” carries a deliberately handmade, body-percussion rhythm and a kind of folk-pop intimacy; the *Big Bang Theory* theme is fast, info-dense, and performatively “clever.” Putting them together could be pure technical play—or it could be a small thesis about how “quirky” mainstream identities are manufactured (craft authenticity on one side, nerd-cosmology compression on the other). Without even a sentence on intent, method (tempo-matching? cut-up? sidechain? rhythmic re-grid?), or what to listen for, the piece risks being received as novelty rather than composition. That may be unfair to the work—but if so, it’s a clarity problem in the framing, not a taste problem in the listener.

The “Works cited” is a welcome gesture, yet it also exposes a common blind spot in remix practice: citation is not the same as permission, and the ethics/legalities of sampling live in that gap. A line or two on whether this is meant as transformative commentary, noncommercial fan labor, or simply study would situate it within the long argument around remix as creativity rather than theft—an argument mapped well by [Lawrence Lessig’s *Remix*](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/298950/remix-by-lawrence-lessig/) and, from a more confrontational angle, the “plunderphonics” tradition associated with [John Oswald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plunderphonics). Even if Daniel doesn’t want to litigate copyright in a music post, acknowledging the constraint is itself part of the artwork’s social context—especially when the source materials are so strongly branded and recognizable.

Finally, the “Made with Audacity…2020” detail is more than trivia: it places the piece in a specific DIY, bedroom-production lineage where tools flatten the distance between consumer and producer. That’s a rich angle to lean into, because it shifts the question from “Is this mashup clever?” to “What kinds of cultural participation does this enable, and what gets lost when participation depends on proprietary catalogs?” A short note connecting the mix to participatory culture—something like the dynamics Henry Jenkins describes in fan remix practices—would turn a tidy artifact into a clearer, more legible cultural statement.
